learningObjectives: Distinguish causal precedence from metric distance.
Recognize irreflexivity, transitivity, and incomparability in a finite strict partial order.
Separate the invariant order represented by a Hasse diagram from the accidental Euclidean geometry of its drawing.
Reject a metric conclusion that lacks the additional hypotheses needed to derive it.
definitions: Event: an element of the set being causally ordered.
Strict partial order: an irreflexive and transitive binary relation.
Comparable events: a pair for which one precedes the other.
Incomparable events: a pair for which neither event precedes the other.
Hasse diagram: a drawing of a finite partial order using covering relations while omitting transitive edges.
Local finiteness: the causal-set condition that every causal interval contains finitely many elements.
notebookPrompt: Create a mathematically serious cinematic lesson titled ‘Order before distance.’ Show how a causal partial order carries precedence, transitivity, and incomparability before any metric is available. Animate a four-event causal diamond, distinguish covering relations from transitive closure, and rotate or distort the drawing so viewers see that drawn Euclidean lengths are not invariant data. Explain that causal-set theory combines causal order with local-finiteness volume information, without claiming every poset determines a unique physical geometry. Foreshadow kinematic space by transforming intervals into points of a derived space. Include the explicit negative control: chain length is not automatically physical distance. Preserve the source packet’s uncertainty and scope limits. Use no anthropomorphic host and no unsupported claims.
humanFrame: The lesson teaches a discipline of inference: relations can determine real structure without determining every quantity. Clearly label definitions, research-program claims, and the later kinematic-space motivation.
assessment: Given a five-event relation, test whether it is a strict partial order, identify incomparable pairs, draw its Hasse diagram, state two order-determined facts, and reject one metric conclusion not warranted by the order alone.
